en:
4.5. The price of a confirmed order covers the whole of the route stated in the order, including the return journey — whether the passenger is carried back or the Partner Driver returns without a passenger — and including waiting at the planned stops and waiting while the passenger is at a destination for which the order provides for a same-day return. Such waiting forms part of performing the route agreed with the Company and is remunerated by the agreed price of the order; no separate payment is due for it.

4.6. Where a confirmed order provides for a same-day return, the Partner Driver is obliged to carry the passenger back to the place stated in the order. That return forms part of the same order and does not constitute a new order.

4.7. The obligation to wait extends only so far as the order states. The Partner Driver is not obliged to wait beyond the stops, the waiting time and the return time stated in the confirmed order. If more waiting is required than the order provides for, or the passenger asks for a change to the route or to the return time, the Partner Driver notifies the Company; the Company agrees the change with the customer and reprices the order before the additional waiting begins. The Partner Driver is not obliged to perform any extension that has not been agreed with the Company in this way.

4.8. The Partner Driver is not entitled to demand any additional sum from a passenger for waiting or for the return journey, or to settle any such sum in the vehicle. Any additional amount is determined and collected solely by the Company, in accordance with clause 6.6 of this agreement, and is settled with the Partner Driver under Article 6.

4.5. დადასტურებული შეკვეთის ღირებულება ფარავს შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ მთელ მარშრუტს, მათ შორის უკან დაბრუნების გზას — მიუხედავად იმისა, უკან მგზავრი ბრუნდება თუ პარტნიორი მძღოლი ბრუნდება მგზავრის გარეშე — და ასევე ლოდინს დაგეგმილ გაჩერებებზე და ლოდინს იმ დროს, როდესაც მგზავრი იმყოფება დანიშნულების ადგილზე, თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას. ასეთი ლოდინი კომპანიასთან შეთანხმებული მარშრუტის შესრულების ნაწილია და ანაზღაურდება შეკვეთის შეთანხმებული ღირებულებით; მისთვის ცალკე გადახდა არ ხდება.

4.6. თუ დადასტურებული შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას, პარტნიორი მძღოლი ვალდებულია მგზავრი უკან დააბრუნოს შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ადგილას. ეს დაბრუნება იმავე შეკვეთის ნაწილია და არ წარმოადგენს ახალ შეკვეთას.

4.7. ლოდინის ვალდებულება ვრცელდება მხოლოდ იმ ფარგლებში, რაც შეკვეთითაა განსაზღვრული. პარტნიორი მძღოლი არ არის ვალდებული, დაელოდოს დადასტურებულ შეკვეთაში მითითებულ გაჩერებებზე, ლოდინის დროსა და დაბრუნების დროზე მეტად. თუ საჭიროა შეკვეთით გათვალისწინებულზე მეტი ლოდინი, ან მგზავრი ითხოვს მარშრუტის ან დაბრუნების დროის ცვლილებას, პარტნიორი მძღოლი ამის შესახებ აცნობებს კომპანიას; კომპანია ცვლილებას ათანხმებს მომხმარებელთან და დამატებითი ლოდინის დაწყებამდე ხელახლა განსაზღვრავს შეკვეთის ღირებულებას. პარტნიორი მძღოლი არ არის ვალდებული, შეასრულოს ისეთი გაგრძელება, რომელიც ამ წესით არ არის შეთანხმებული კომპანიასთან.

4.8. პარტნიორი მძღოლი უფლებამოსილი არ არის, მგზავრს მოსთხოვოს დამატებითი თანხა ლოდინის ან უკან დაბრუნებისთვის, ან ასეთი თანხა ავტომობილში მოაგვაროს. ნებისმიერ დამატებით თანხას განსაზღვრავს და იღებს მხოლოდ კომპანია, წინამდებარე ხელშეკრულების 6.6. მუხლის შესაბამისად, ხოლო პარტნიორ მძღოლთან ანგარიშსწორება ხდება მე-6 მუხლის წესით.
rationale:
The public site promises travellers, in all three languages, that "Planned stops and waiting are included in the price" (src/lib/i18n/en.ts "home.why3b" / "search.stopsNote", and the ka mirrors) and that on a round trip "the driver stays with you and brings you back" ("search.roundTripNote"). The published driver agreement had no counterpart obligation at all, so the promise ran against a driver who had never agreed to it. These paragraphs put the same promise into Article 4, where the order-performance duties already live (4.3 attend, perform the agreed route; 4.4 no transfer).

They state what the pricing engine already does rather than inventing a new commercial position: a round trip is priced with distance counted in both directions, and a one-way is priced including the driver's empty return leg. 4.5 therefore opens by saying the price covers the whole stated route including the return journey "whether the passenger is carried back or the Partner Driver returns without a passenger" — which is exactly the two branches of the pricing model — and then says waiting is part of performing that route and is remunerated by that same price. The driver is being told what he is already paid for, not asked to absorb anything.

4.6 answers Sandro's second gap: it makes the same-day return part of the same order, so it cannot be recharacterised as a second job to be renegotiated at the destination, and equally cannot be treated by the Company as a second order for commission purposes.

4.8 aligns with the existing 6.6 ("The driver is not entitled to demand any additional sum from a customer, other than for additional services determined in advance by the Company") and cross-references it in the same style as 6.5's reference to clause 2.1.7. It closes the loop the driver cares about most: money never changes hands in the car, and the extra he is owed reaches him through the ordinary Article 6 settlement rather than as cash he has to argue for.

Independent-contractor safety: nothing here directs how, when or with what the driver works generally. Every obligation is triggered by a confirmed order that 4.2 leaves him free to decline, is owed to the Company as the counterparty rather than to a passenger giving instructions, and is bounded by the order's own terms — the shape of a service obligation under a specific commission, not of an employment instruction. 4.7 in particular gives the driver a right to refuse, which an employment clause would not.

Both language versions carry the same four paragraphs with the same numbering and the same content; the Georgian uses the established vocabulary of the agreement (პარტნიორი მძღოლი, დადასტურებული შეკვეთა, ვალდებულია, უფლებამოსილი არ არის) and of the public site (დაგეგმილი გაჩერებები, ლოდინი, უკან დაბრუნება), so a driver signing either copy signs the same thing.

Placement note for whoever applies this: the agreement text lives in db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql (Georgian Article 4 around line 285, English around line 469), rendered through C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\contract.ts. Because the signature stores a SHA-256 of the resolved body, this must go out as a NEW contract version rather than an edit to the published one — otherwise every existing driver signature stops matching the text it attests to.
boundedness: The obligation is bounded in four separate ways, and 4.7 exists for nothing else. First, it attaches only to a confirmed order the driver chose to accept under 4.2 — there is no standing duty to be available. Second, its extent is fixed by that order's own contents: "The obligation to wait extends only so far as the order states", and the driver "is not obliged to wait beyond the stops, the waiting time and the return time stated in the confirmed order". Nothing in 4.5 or 4.6 imports a duty wider than the order text; 4.5 covers waiting at the planned stops and at a destination "for which the order provides for a same-day return", so an order that provides for neither creates neither duty. Third, more waiting is not something the passenger can impose in the car: it is notified to the Company, agreed by the Company with the customer, and repriced by the Company BEFORE the additional waiting begins — so the driver is never in the position of working first and arguing about payment afterwards. Fourth, the driver's escape is stated affirmatively rather than left to implication: he "is not obliged to perform any extension that has not been agreed with the Company in this way", which means an unagreed extension carries no breach exposure under Article 11 and no deactivation risk. So the worst case for a driver is bounded by a number he saw before he accepted the job.

scores.verdict: Strong, well-targeted drafting that closes a genuine gap Sandro correctly identified, and it is safe on the independent-contractor axis — but it must not ship as written. Two defects need fixing first, one of them in the governing language. Fit and register: excellent. Numbering (4.5-4.8) is correct, the vocabulary matches ("the Partner Driver", "is obliged to", "a confirmed order"; "პარტნიორი მძღოლი", "ვალდებულია", "დადასტურებული შეკვეთა"), and 4.8's cross-reference to 6.6 is to a real clause (0015 line 499 EN / 315 KA) in the same citation style 6.5 already uses for 2.1.7. Conflict with 4.2/4.3: none. Every duty in 4.5-4.8 attaches only after a confirmed order, which 4.2 leaves the driver free to decline, and 4.5 anchors waiting inside "the route agreed with the Company" — 4.3's own phrase — so it extends 4.3 rather than competing with it. Contractor characterisation: not undermined. The obligations are owed to the Company as counterparty, are bounded by the commission's own terms, and say nothing about how, when or with what the driver works generally. 4.7's affirmative right of refusal is the strongest single piece of contractor evidence in Article 4. 4.8 adds no new price control — it applies the already-published 6.6 to a specific case. Commercial accuracy: verified. engine.ts:147 counts distance in both directions on a round trip and engine.ts:178 drops deadhead only then, so 4.5's "whether the passenger is carried back or the Partner Driver returns without a passenger" is a faithful statement of the two pricing branches, not a new commercial position. Boundedness — where it fails. The bound holds for a round trip, because returnAt is a real stored order term (offers.ts:210, booking.ts:133). It does not hold for a one-way with planned stops. The itinerary stores stops as bare location slugs (offers.ts:208) and the engine takes extraStops only as a count against a flat per-stop fee; no order field anywhere states a waiting duration. So "the waiting time... stated in the confirmed order" names a term no order contains, and "beyond the stops... stated in the order" bounds the number of stops rather than the time spent at each. A passenger who spends three hours at a listed stop is not asking for anything "beyond the stops stated", so 4.5 obliges the driver to wait and 4.7 does not release him. That is the exact indefinite-waiting failure mode 4.7 was written to prevent. The Georgian defect is independent and arguably worse, because Georgian governs (contract.ts header). Overall: the substance is right and the drafting is careful; publish as a new version only after the two fixes below.
defects: Boundedness fails on one-way orders (4.5 + 4.7). 4.7 bounds the duty by "the stops, the waiting time and the return time stated in the confirmed order", but of those three only the return time exists as an order term: db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql orders carry returnAt (src/lib/offers.ts:210, src/lib/booking.ts:133), while stops are bare location slugs (src/lib/offers.ts:208) and src/lib/pricing/engine.ts takes only `extraStops` as a COUNT against a flat perStopFeeMinor — there is no waiting-duration field in the itinerary, the quote inputs, or the engine. "Beyond the stops stated in the order" therefore bounds how MANY stops, not how LONG at each. On a one-way with three planned stops, a passenger who takes three hours at stop two is not requesting anything beyond the stops the order states, so 4.5 makes that waiting part of performing the route and 4.7 grants no release. A driver can be argued into indefinite waiting at a planned stop. Fix: either add a stated waiting time per stop to the order (and cite it as it actually exists), or amend 4.7 to "...beyond the stops, the times and the return time stated in the confirmed order, and where the order states no waiting time for a stop, beyond a reasonable time for the stated purpose of that stop."

Scope ambiguity in the GOVERNING Georgian text of 4.5. English attaches the same-day-return condition restrictively to the destination ("waiting while the passenger is at a destination FOR WHICH the order provides for a same-day return"). The Georgian moves it to a trailing conditional — "...მგზავრი იმყოფება დანიშნულების ადგილზე, თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას" — which on its face can condition the whole sentence, i.e. the price covers the route, the return AND waiting at planned stops only if the order provides for a same-day return. Under that reading a one-way order's planned-stop waiting is not covered by the price at all, which inverts the customer promise at src/lib/i18n/ka.ts:36,70 and defeats the clause's purpose. Since src/lib/contract.ts records that Georgian governs and a driver may sign either copy, the two versions do not reliably say the same thing. Fix by making the qualifier attributive: "...ლოდინს იმ დროს, როდესაც მგზავრი იმყოფება იმ დანიშნულების ადგილზე, რომლის მიმართაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას."

4.7's escape mechanism binds only the driver, not the Company. "The Partner Driver notifies the Company; the Company agrees the change with the customer and reprices the order" is drafted in the present indicative as narration, imposing no duty and no time limit on the Company to respond — unlike Article 8, where every Company duty is expressed as one. The driver's only lawful route to paid extra waiting therefore depends entirely on the Company answering, and on routes the platform actually sells (Ushguli, Tusheti) it may not answer at all. Add a Company obligation to respond without delay, or a fallback letting the driver wait and be repriced afterwards on his own record of the actual waiting.

The rationale overstates 4.7's protection against Article 11, and the clause does not close the gap. The claim that an unagreed extension "carries no breach exposure under Article 11 and no deactivation risk" is true of 11.1 (breach of an obligation) but not of 11.7, which is not breach-based: "Systematic lateness, cancellation, customer complaints and/or breaches of safety rules... may give grounds for reviewing the driver's status or ending the cooperation." A driver who properly exercises his 4.7 refusal and leaves a passenger at a destination will reliably generate the customer complaint that triggers 11.7. 4.7 should state that a refusal properly exercised under it is not a ground for review under 11.7.

4.5's closing "no separate payment is due for it" is unqualified and sits before 4.7, so it can be read as denying separate payment for waiting even where 4.7 has repriced the order. Add "...save where the order is repriced under clause 4.7" (and the Georgian mirror).

Minor: 4.6's "the place stated in the order" is not an order field. The itinerary stores origin, stops and destination (src/lib/offers.ts:206-211); a round trip returns to the origin, and no separate return destination is captured. Prefer "back to the place of departure, or to such other place as the order states."

scores.verdict: The Georgian is correct, formal legal Georgian and says materially the same thing as the English: the same four obligations with the same four limits, in the agreement's established vocabulary. Verb morphology and case government are sound throughout (optative after ვალდებულია; nominative მგზავრი under series-II დააბრუნოს; dative objects of ფარავს; correct shared-postposition coordination in ლოდინის დროსა და დაბრუნების დროზე and ლოდინის ან უკან დაბრუნებისთვის). No obligation, and no limit on an obligation, exists in one language version and not the other, so a driver signing either copy signs the same bargain. The defects are one genuine ambiguity in 4.7 that should be fixed before publication, plus a handful of register and internal-consistency nits — none of which shift the commercial position. Approve subject to the 4.7 rewording.
defects: 4.7, most serious: 'არ არის ვალდებული, დაელოდოს დადასტურებულ შეკვეთაში მითითებულ გაჩერებებზე, ლოდინის დროსა და დაბრუნების დროზე მეტად' is ambiguous because -ზე carries both a locative and a comparative reading and the disambiguating 'მეტად' sits at the very end of a three-item list. Read locatively and stopping short, it says the driver is not obliged to wait AT the stops — the exact opposite of 4.5 and 4.6. Suggested fix: 'არ არის ვალდებული, ლოდინი გააგრძელოს დადასტურებულ შეკვეთაში მითითებული გაჩერებების, ლოდინის დროისა და დაბრუნების დროის ფარგლებს გარეთ'.

4.7 lexical: 'მეტად' expresses degree, not duration. For 'wait beyond/longer' Georgian requires 'მეტ ხანს' (or a ფარგლებს გარეთ construction). Note the very next sentence gets this right with 'შეკვეთით გათვალისწინებულზე მეტი ლოდინი', which makes the inconsistency visible within one paragraph.

4.5 scope ambiguity: the conditional 'თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას' is placed at the end of a two-item list and can be attached either to the nearest clause (the intended reading, matching the English restrictive relative 'a destination for which the order provides for a same-day return') or to the whole sentence, in which case waiting at planned stops would also be covered only on same-day-return orders. The English relative clause cannot be misread this way. Fix by restructuring: '...და ლოდინს დანიშნულების ადგილზე იმ შეკვეთის შემთხვევაში, რომელიც ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას'.

4.8 register: 'ასეთი თანხა ავტომობილში მოაგვაროს' is informal. მოგვარება ('to sort out') is not the register of the surrounding text, which uses ანგარიშსწორება (6.5). Prefer 'ან განახორციელოს ასეთი თანხის ანგარიშსწორება ავტომობილში' or 'ან ადგილზე მიიღოს ასეთი თანხა'. The latter would also close a small gap shared with the English: 'settle' does not clearly prohibit merely accepting money a passenger volunteers.

4.8 cross-reference collision: '6.6. მუხლის შესაბამისად' and 'მე-6 მუხლის წესით' appear in the same sentence denoting two different levels of the document (a sub-clause and the whole Article). The agreement is already internally inconsistent here — 6.5 writes '2.1.7. მუხლით' for a sub-clause while 3.3 writes '3.2. პუნქტით' — so following the 6.5 precedent is defensible, but doing so in the same breath as a true მუხლი reference is confusing. Use '6.6. პუნქტის შესაბამისად ... მე-6 მუხლის წესით'.

4.8 consistency with the clause it cross-references: the existing 6.6 states the driver-side prohibition as 'მძღოლს არ აქვს უფლება'. 4.8 uses 'უფლებამოსილი არ არის'. Both are correct legal Georgian (and უფლებამოსილია is used of the Company at 3.3), but since 4.8 expressly incorporates 6.6, matching its formula would be tighter.

4.7 collocation: 'შეასრულოს ისეთი გაგრძელება' is odd Georgian — one does not 'perform a continuation'. Prefer naming the thing: 'შეასრულოს ისეთი დამატებითი ლოდინი ან მარშრუტის ცვლილება, რომელიც ამ წესით არ არის შეთანხმებული კომპანიასთან'.

4.7 register: 'შეკვეთითაა განსაზღვრული' uses the fused copula. Acceptable in general Georgian but slightly below the register of the surrounding contract; 'შეკვეთით არის განსაზღვრული' is preferable. Relatedly, 'იმ ფარგლებში, რაც' leaves the relative pronoun in the nominative against a postpositional antecedent; 'იმდენად, რამდენადაც' or 'იმ ფარგლებით, რაც' is stricter.

4.5 nuance loss: the English passive 'whether the passenger is carried back' keeps the driver as the implied agent; the Georgian 'უკან მგზავრი ბრუნდება' is intransitive and agentless ('the passenger returns'). No obligation turns on it, since the duty to carry is imposed by 4.6, but 'დაბრუნდება თუ არა მგზავრი პარტნიორი მძღოლის მიერ' would preserve the parallel. Word order 'უკან მგზავრი ბრუნდება' is also slightly marked; 'მგზავრი ბრუნდება უკან' is more natural.

4.5 minor: 'მისთვის ცალკე გადახდა არ ხდება' is descriptive ('does not happen') where the English 'no separate payment is due' is normative. 'ცალკე გადახდა არ ხორციელდება' matches 6.5's ხორციელდება and the register of an obligation-defining sentence.

Terminology drift on 'stated in the order': 4.5 and 4.6 use 'შეკვეთით განსაზღვრული' while 4.7 uses 'შეკვეთაში მითითებული', and the existing 4.3 uses 'მითითებული' for 'stated'. Harmless as to meaning but worth unifying on მითითებული. Likewise 4.6's 'ადგილას' against 4.3's 'ადგილზე'.

scores.verdict: Structurally the right fix in the right place, and contractor-safe: every duty is triggered by a confirmed order the driver may decline under 4.2, is owed to the Company rather than to a passenger giving instructions, and 4.7 states an affirmative right of refusal — nothing here reads as an employment instruction. 4.6 matches the pricing engine exactly (src/lib/pricing/engine.ts:147,178 — a round trip bills distance and driving time in both directions and drops the deadhead line entirely, so the passenger-carrying return is already paid at full rate; the driver is being told what he is paid for, not asked to absorb anything). The prohibition on charging the passenger is directionally correct and correctly routed to the Company. But it must not ship as drafted: 4.8 as written puts a driver in technical breach on every cash booking, 4.5 overstates what the one-way price covers in a way the driver's own fare breakdown contradicts, and the same-day limitation leaves the site's round-trip promise unbacked for overnight round trips the product sells today. Revise 4.8 and the return-journey sentence of 4.5, decide the multi-day question, then publish as a new contract version (db/migrations/0016_contract_party_is_the_company.sql:30 already enforces that).
defects: 4.8 contradicts the platform's own cash mode and would make lawful conduct a breach. The site sells CASH bookings ('Cash to the driver' / 'Pay the agreed amount in Georgian lari at the end of the trip', C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\i18n\en.ts:278-279, faq.a8 line 222), and C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\booking.ts:370-375 posts the ledger on the premise that 'The driver collected the whole fare'. So on a cash order the driver necessarily settles the fare in the vehicle. 4.8's 'Any additional amount is determined and collected solely by the Company' and the flat ban on settling 'any such sum in the vehicle' are therefore false as to collection and, read literally, make a driver who takes the Company-repriced cash fare a breaching party. Fix by separating determination from collection: 'Any additional amount is determined solely by the Company. Where the order is paid in cash, the Partner Driver collects only the amount stated in the Company's system; settlement with the Partner Driver is made under Article 6.' (KA: 'ნებისმიერ დამატებით თანხას განსაზღვრავს მხოლოდ კომპანია; ნაღდი ანგარიშსწორების შეკვეთისას პარტნიორი მძღოლი იღებს მხოლოდ კომპანიის სისტემაში მითითებულ თანხას…')

4.8's cross-reference asserts a consistency with 6.6 that does not exist. 6.6 (migration line 499 / KA line 315) expressly permits demanding an additional sum from a customer 'for additional services determined in advance by the Company'; 4.8 forbids demanding any additional sum for waiting or the return. That is a narrowing, not an application, so 'in accordance with clause 6.6' is inaccurate. Use 'notwithstanding the exception in clause 6.6' (KA: 'წინამდებარე ხელშეკრულების 6.6. მუხლით გათვალისწინებული გამონაკლისის მიუხედავად'), or amend 6.6 in the same new version.

4.5 overstates the one-way case and is contradicted by the driver's own quote breakdown. The empty return is recovered only at a share: defaultDeadheadRecovery in C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\offers.ts:490-496 returns 10% under 30 km, 35% under 100, 55% under 250, 70% beyond (table default 5000 bps, db/migrations/0001_baseline.sql:130), and engine.ts:185 prints that share to the driver as '… km empty return, 35% recovered'. Saying the price 'covers the whole of the route stated in the order, including the return journey — whether … the Partner Driver returns without a passenger' tells the driver he is fully paid for a leg his fare line says is 10-70% recovered — in the clause whose whole purpose is restoring trust. (It also conflates: on a one-way the empty return is not part of 'the route stated in the order'.) Say the price 'is calculated to include the Partner Driver's return journey, whether the passenger is carried back or the Partner Driver returns without a passenger, as determined in the Company's system' and let the breakdown speak for the amount.

Scope gap: the obligations attach only to a 'same-day return', but the product sells multi-day round trips and prices them the same way. offers.ts:192 sets roundTrip on any returnAt later than travelAt, offers.ts:195-198 counts crossed day boundaries as nights and charges the overnight fee, and the return input in C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\components\search-form.tsx:261-264 has only min={when} — no same-day cap. search.roundTripNote ('The driver stays with you and brings you back') is shown for every round trip. So an overnight Kazbegi or three-day Svaneti round trip is priced in both directions, promised to the customer, and still has no counterpart duty in Article 4 — exactly Sandro's gap, left open for the longer bookings where it costs most. Either extend 4.5/4.6 to 'a return provided for by the order' (with 4.7 and the overnight terms doing the bounding) or cap the return picker to the same day.

The bound in 4.7 is only as strong as what the order states, and the order states no waiting duration for intermediate stops. The stored itinerary (offers.ts:206-212) is {origin, stops: string[], destination, roundTrip?, returnAt?} — returnAt does bound the destination wait, but stops are bare place slugs with a flat perStopFeeMinor (engine.ts:196-199) and no duration. So 4.5 obliges waiting 'at the planned stops' while 4.7's limit ('the waiting time … stated in the confirmed order') has no referent for those stops: requirement (d) is met for the return leg and empty for stop waiting. Add a residual standard — 'or, where the order states no duration for a stop, for the duration agreed with the Company' (KA: 'ხოლო თუ შეკვეთა გაჩერების ხანგრძლივობას არ განსაზღვრავს — კომპანიასთან შეთანხმებული ხანგრძლივობით') — or add a per-stop duration to the order model.

4.7 imposes on the Company a real-time repricing duty the system cannot presently perform: it requires the Company to agree the change with the customer and reprice the order 'before the additional waiting begins', but there is no in-flight amendment path for a confirmed booking — the only repricing found is the marketplace band change in C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\app\admin\actions.ts:824-830, which affects future quotes. Either build the booking-amendment path before this version goes live or soften to 'the Company agrees the change with the customer and confirms the revised price to the Partner Driver before the additional waiting begins'.

Georgian 4.5 has a scope ambiguity the English does not. English restricts the condition to the destination wait ('waiting while the passenger is at a destination for which the order provides for a same-day return'); the Georgian puts it as a trailing conditional — '…და ლოდინს იმ დროს, როდესაც მგზავრი იმყოფება დანიშნულების ადგილზე, თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას' — which can be read as qualifying the whole preceding enumeration, including coverage of the route and of stop waiting. Since a driver may sign either copy, mirror the English relative clause: '…და ლოდინს იმ დანიშნულების ადგილზე, რომლისთვისაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას.' (Separately, 4.8's 'ავტომობილში მოაგვაროს' is below the register of the surrounding text; 'ავტომობილში განახორციელოს ანგარიშსწორება' fits. The '6.6. მუხლის' form is fine — it follows the existing 6.5 reference to '2.1.7. მუხლით'.)

scores.verdict: Structurally sound and stylistically correct, but not publishable as drafted — both sides find real holes. The numbering, register, vocabulary, cross-reference (6.6 does exist in the driver agreement at db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:499 / :315, and Article 6 settlement and 4.2's right to decline exist as relied on) and the independent-contractor posture are all fine, and 4.8 genuinely closes the money-in-the-car gap. But (1) the clause obliges the return ONLY on a same-day return, while multi-day round trips are a first-class, fully priced product the site sells with "the driver stays with you and brings you back" — leaving a passenger legally abandonable at Batumi on a Friday-to-Sunday booking; (2) the entire bounding mechanism in 4.7 is anchored to "the waiting time and the return time stated in the confirmed order", and neither of those data exist anywhere in the system — no dwell/wait field, no return_at column, and the driver portal shows neither — so the duty is either zero minutes (driver's reading, which defeats the site's "planned stops and waiting are included" for every stop-bearing order) or unbounded (which defeats 4.7's own promise); (3) no affirmative duty to wait is ever actually imposed — 4.5 is a pricing characterisation and 4.7 is a cap on a duty that must still be inferred from 4.3. Fixing 4.6's same-day limitation, giving waiting a stated default where the order is silent (and adding the field to the order), and adding one operative "is obliged to wait" sentence would take this to publishable.
defects: MULTI-DAY ROUND TRIP HAS NO RETURN OBLIGATION (passenger's lawyer, serious). 4.5 and 4.6 both condition on "a same-day return" / "იმავე დღეს დაბრუნება". But src/lib/offers.ts:192 treats ANY returnAt later than travelAt as a round trip, src/lib/offers.ts:195-198 charges nights = floor(days between) with an overnight fee, offers.ts:301 sets bookedDays = nights + 1 so the per-day floor applies, roundTripWindow (src/lib/offers.ts:111) blocks the driver's calendar across the whole stay, and src/lib/booking.ts:196-203 writes the return leg with an explicit day_index. src/app/[locale]/search/page.tsx:84 accepts a free return datetime with no same-day constraint. So a Tbilisi-Batumi booking returning two days later is priced for both directions plus two nights plus two day floors, and the driver is under no obligation whatsoever under 4.6 to carry the passenger back, nor is that waiting covered by 4.5. He can lawfully drop them and drive home, then treat Sunday as a new order to renegotiate — exactly what 4.6 was written to prevent. "search.roundTripNote" (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:607, ka.ts:588, ru.ts:588) promises "the driver stays with you and brings you back" with no same-day limit.

THE BOUNDING FIELDS DO NOT EXIST (both lawyers, serious). 4.7 caps the duty at "the stops, the waiting time and the return time stated in the confirmed order". Of those three anchors only stops exist. There is no waiting/dwell field anywhere: the itinerary written at src/lib/offers.ts:206-211 is {origin, stops[], destination, roundTrip, returnAt} and the leg rows at src/lib/booking.ts:202-204 carry only position, location_id, label, day_index. There is no return_at column in any migration (grep over db/migrations/*.sql returns nothing), so the booking stores only a return DAY index, not a time. Driver's lawyer: the order states no waiting time and no return time, therefore my obligation beyond them is nil — I stop at Ananuri, the passenger gets out, I am entitled to leave, and I have complied with every word. Passenger's lawyer: "home.why3b"/"search.stopsNote" (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:42,77 and the ka/ru mirrors) promise "Planned stops and waiting are included in the price. You pay nothing extra", and this clause backs that promise with a duration that is never stated. The rationale's claim that "the worst case for a driver is bounded by a number he saw before he accepted the job" is false: there is no such number in the system.

THE DRIVER IS NEVER SHOWN THE RETURN TIME (both lawyers). The customer IS shown one — src/app/[locale]/search/page.tsx:185 renders "Return leg: <full date, time>" and src/app/[locale]/checkout/page.tsx:119-122 repeats it — but it is never persisted onto the booking and the driver's own order list (src/app/driver/orders/page.tsx:38-44,156) selects and displays only service_start_at and the concatenated leg labels. So the two sides of the same order are looking at different documents, and a clause whose limits are defined by "the return time stated in the confirmed order" refers to something the obligated party cannot see. Any dispute about whether the driver waited long enough is unresolvable from the record.

NO AFFIRMATIVE DUTY TO WAIT IS EVER IMPOSED (drafting, serious given the purpose). 4.5 is cast entirely in the descriptive/pricing register — waiting "forms part of performing the route" and "is remunerated by the agreed price"; 4.6 imposes a duty only to carry the passenger back; 4.7 is a negative cap. Nowhere does the text say the Partner Driver is obliged to wait. A driver's lawyer will characterise 4.5 as a consideration clause and argue the only operative duty is 4.3's "perform the route agreed with the Company", which is what already existed and which Sandro correctly said says nothing about waiting. 4.7 then caps an obligation the instrument never creates. One sentence — "The Partner Driver is obliged to wait at the planned stops and, where the order provides for a return, at the destination, for the time stated in the order" — is missing.

4.5 OVERSTATES WHAT THE PRICE ACTUALLY COVERS (driver's lawyer, moderate). The clause has the driver acknowledge the price covers the return journey "whether the passenger is carried back or the Partner Driver returns without a passenger", and covers waiting. Neither is fully true in the engine. On a one-way the empty return is recovered only in part: defaultDeadheadRecovery at src/lib/offers.ts:490-496 returns 10% under 30 km, 35% under 100, 55% under 250, 70% beyond — never 100%. And waiting has no priced component at all: src/lib/pricing/engine.ts:147-206 bills distance x directions, drive minutes x directions, perStopFeeMinor x extraStops, and overnightFeeMinor x nights; there is no wait line, and on a same-day round trip nights = 0 so bookedDays = 0 (src/lib/offers.ts:301) and the minimumDayFareMinor floor never applies. A driver who sits six hours at Kazbegi on a same-day return is paid for two drive legs and nothing else. Getting him to sign that the fee "covers" that waiting is an admission the rationale wrongly describes as merely reciting what he is already paid.

WAITING IS BOUNDED IN TIME BUT NOT IN PLACE (passenger's lawyer, moderate). Nothing requires the driver to remain with the vehicle, at the destination, or contactable during the waiting period. A driver can satisfy every word of 4.5-4.7 while spending the wait in the next town, provided he is back by a return time the order does not state. "search.roundTripNote" tells the traveller "the driver stays with you".

4.7 HAS NO FALLBACK WHEN THE COMPANY CANNOT BE REACHED (passenger's lawyer). Extra waiting requires notification to the Company, agreement with the customer and repricing "before the additional waiting begins", with no response deadline and no rule for the common Georgian case of no signal in Tusheti or Svaneti at 22:00. The driver is expressly "not obliged to perform any extension that has not been agreed", so on the words he may depart while the customer is still inside and the Company's phone is ringing. Good for the driver, but it means the customer-facing promise fails precisely in the situations it matters.

4.8's CROSS-REFERENCE SLIGHTLY MISSTATES 6.6 (drafting nit). 6.6 (db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:499) prohibits demanding extra sums "other than for additional services determined in advance by the Company" — i.e. it expressly contemplates the driver collecting for pre-approved extras. 4.8 says any additional amount is "determined and collected solely by the Company, in accordance with clause 6.6", which narrows 6.6 rather than following it, and does so for waiting repriced mid-trip, which by definition was not "determined in advance". It works as lex specialis but "in accordance with" papers over the change; "notwithstanding clause 6.6" or an explicit carve-out would be honest. Note also 6.5 permits cash settlement generally.

GEORGIAN/ENGLISH DIVERGENCES (minor but real, since a driver may sign either). (a) 4.5 English "no separate payment is due for it" is normative; Georgian "მისთვის ცალკე გადახდა არ ხდება" is descriptive ("no separate payment is made") — a statement of practice, not of entitlement, and weaker against a driver claiming one. (b) 4.5 English attaches the same-day condition to the particular destination ("a destination for which the order provides"); the Georgian attaches it to the order as a whole ("თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს"), which diverges on a multi-stop itinerary. (c) "wait beyond the stops" / "დაელოდოს ... გაჩერებებზე ... მეტად" is clumsy in both: one does not wait "beyond a stop", and the Georgian construction invites the reading "wait more than at the stops".

en:
4.5. Waiting at the stops stated in a confirmed order, and waiting while the passenger is at a destination where the order provides for a return on the same day, forms part of performing the route agreed with the Company. Where a confirmed order provides for a return on the same day, the Partner Driver is obliged to carry the passenger back; that return journey forms part of the same order and does not constitute a new order. The price of such an order is determined under clause 6.1 with the return distance included, and the remuneration payable to the Partner Driver under Article 6 covers that waiting and that return journey.

4.6. The Partner Driver's obligation to wait extends only to the stops and to the waiting time stated in the order, and to no greater extent. Where the passenger requests waiting beyond what the order states, the Partner Driver notifies the Company; such additional waiting is performed only where the Company has agreed it and has repriced the order accordingly, and the repriced amount is settled through the Company under Article 6. Where no extension has been agreed with the Company, the Partner Driver is not obliged to continue waiting after the time stated in the order has expired.

4.7. In accordance with clause 6.6, the Partner Driver is not entitled to request or to accept any additional sum from the passenger for waiting or for the return journey, whether for the waiting stated in the order or for additional waiting agreed with the Company. Whether to accept an order that provides for waiting or for a same-day return remains a matter for the Partner Driver under clause 4.2.

rationale:
The gap is exact and one-directional: the site tells travellers in all three languages that "Planned stops and waiting are included in the price. You pay nothing extra." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:42 and :77, ka.ts:36 and :70, ru.ts:36 and :70), that "Waiting at them is not charged extra" (en.ts:194 / ka.ts:182), and for round trips that "The driver stays with you and brings you back" (en.ts:607 / ka.ts:588) — while the driver agreement, Article 4 of the DRIVER body in C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\db\migrations\0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql (Georgian at lines 285-293, English at lines 469-477), obliges the driver only to attend and "perform the route agreed with the Company". Nothing in it mentions waiting or bringing the passenger back, so the promise had no counterpart on the driver side.

Each drafted phrase answers one line of the public copy. "Waiting at the stops stated in a confirmed order... forms part of performing the route agreed with the Company" attaches the waiting to the existing 4.3 obligation rather than creating a new one, which is what makes "included in the price" true rather than merely asserted. "Where a confirmed order provides for a return on the same day, the Partner Driver is obliged to carry the passenger back; that return journey forms part of the same order and does not constitute a new order" is the driver-side counterpart of "brings you back", and the "same order" wording forecloses the reading that the return is a fresh job to be renegotiated at the roadside. "You pay nothing extra" is made good by 4.7, which does not invent a new prohibition but points at the one already in 6.6 and names the two things the site promises for free.

The clause writes down what the fee already covers rather than adding unpaid work: the engine prices a round trip with distance counted in both directions and prices a one-way including the driver's empty return, and DECISIONS.md ("Round trips are priced as one journey, not two") records that a wait-and-return books one driver for the whole span with the deadhead recovery removed because the driver comes home loaded. 4.5 therefore says the price is determined under 6.1 "with the return distance included" and that the Article 6 remuneration covers the waiting and the return — the driver can read the economic justification inside the clause that binds him.

Contractor status is preserved deliberately. The obligation is framed as the scope of an order the driver has already accepted, not as an instruction about how he spends his time; nothing directs his conduct at the destination; and the closing sentence of 4.7 sends the reader back to 4.2, so the answer to "must I take wait-and-return work?" stays no. This also matches 1.4, under which the Partner Driver independently manages which orders he agrees to perform.

The repricing route is the Company, never the car: 4.6 requires notification to the Company and settlement through it under Article 6, which keeps the money flow consistent with 6.5 and 6.6 and prevents cash side-deals that Article 5 already treats as a breach.

Operationally, this is a change to the contract body text in both language blocks of the DRIVER agreement; since signatures are bound to a version and to a SHA-256 of the exact text read (src\lib\contract.ts), it needs a new contract version row rather than an edit in place, and drivers who signed the previous version — Sandro included — would sign the new one.
boundedness: Boundedness is carried by 4.6 and is threefold. First, a stated ceiling: "The Partner Driver's obligation to wait extends only to the stops and to the waiting time stated in the order, and to no greater extent" — the order, not the passenger's convenience, fixes the extent, so an order that states no waiting period creates no waiting obligation beyond the stops it lists. Second, an express release: "Where no extension has been agreed with the Company, the Partner Driver is not obliged to continue waiting after the time stated in the order has expired" — the driver is free once the stated time runs out, which is what makes the obligation finite rather than merely qualified. Third, the only route past that ceiling runs through the Company, which must both agree the additional waiting and reprice the order before it is performed, so extra time cannot be imposed by the passenger in the car, and any time actually added is paid time. The word "obliged" in 4.5 attaches to the return journey and to waiting only within those limits; there is no residual "as reasonably required" or "until the passenger is ready" language anywhere in the three paragraphs.

scores.verdict:
Sound drafting that closes the real gap, fits Article 4 cleanly, and does not endanger contractor status — but its boundedness rests on an order field that does not exist, and it contradicts one line of the public copy it claims to answer. Adopt after fixing the anchor in 4.6.

WHAT WORKS

Fit and register. Appending 4.5–4.7 renumbers nothing and no clause elsewhere cross-references Article 4 beyond 4.2, which is preserved. Vocabulary matches the body exactly ("the Partner Driver", "the Company", "a confirmed order", "is obliged to"; "პარტნიორი მძღოლი", "კომპანია", "ვალდებულია", "დადასტურებული შეკვეთა"). Cross-reference style matches too: English "clause 6.1" tracks existing "clause 3.2"/"clause 2.1.7" (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\db\migrations\0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:464, :448), and Georgian "6.1. მუხლის" tracks the existing "2.1.7. მუხლით" in 6.5 (line ~316). The two versions are substantively equivalent sentence by sentence; I found no divergence of obligation between them.

No conflict with 4.2 or 4.3. Attaching the waiting to "performing the route agreed with the Company" makes 4.5 an interpretation of the 4.3 obligation rather than a new duty, which is the right structural move — it is what makes "included in the price" a contractual fact rather than an assertion. The closing sentence of 4.7 expressly returns the acceptance decision to 4.2, consistent with 1.4 (line 430).

Contractor status is preserved. Nothing directs the driver's conduct during the wait, no place-of-work or hours language, no reporting-to language; the obligation is scope-of-order, which is how a services contract binds a contractor. This reads as a term of service, not an instruction to a subordinate.

The economics claim is true in the code. engine.ts:166 bills loaded distance at directions × km (both directions on a round trip); engine.ts:178 zeroes the deadhead on a round trip because the driver comes home loaded; offers.ts:109-117 (roundTripWindow) blocks the driver from pickup to return, so the whole span is already sold once. So "the remuneration payable under Article 6 covers that waiting and that return journey" is accurate, not aspirational — the clause writes down paid work.

Money routing is right: 4.6/4.7 keep repricing and settlement inside the Company, consistent with 6.5, 6.6 and Article 5's anti-side-deal rule.

THE MATERIAL PROBLEM

4.6 pegs the ceiling to "the waiting time stated in the order", and nothing in the system ever states one. A booking records stops (stopSlugs) and, for a round trip, a return time (returnAt — src\lib\booking.ts:132-135); the pricing engine takes extraStops as a count and nights, and has no waiting-duration input at all (src\lib\pricing\engine.ts:198-204). So the release sentence — "not obliged to continue waiting after the time stated in the order has expired" — is keyed to a trigger that in practice never fires, because no time is stated. The drafter's reading (no stated time, therefore no obligation) is defensible but is left to inference, and a company arguing from 4.5 ("waiting while the passenger is at a destination ... forms part of performing the route") has room to press for open-ended waiting at a stop. Requirement (d) is met on the page and only half met against the system.

Fix by pegging the cap to what an order actually records: the stops it lists and, for a same-day return, the return time (returnAt) — plus a stated default allowance per stop where the order gives none. Suggested English for the first sentence of 4.6: "The Partner Driver's obligation to wait extends only to the stops stated in the order and, where the order provides for a return on the same day, until the return time stated in the order, and to no greater extent; where the order states no waiting period for a stop, the obligation at that stop is [30] minutes." Georgian: "...მხოლოდ შეკვეთაში მითითებულ გაჩერებებზე და, თუ შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას, შეკვეთაში მითითებულ დაბრუნების დრომდე..." Then the release sentence has something to expire against.

Everything else is second-order and fixable in a line each: the FAQ contradiction (see defects), the "in accordance with clause 6.6" over-label in 4.7, the pricing rule attributed to 6.1 that 6.1 does not contain, and the fact that the repricing route 4.6 mandates has no priced mechanism today (DECISIONS.md, "Hourly hire is an inquiry, not a price": no per-hour rates exist in driver price plans), so "has repriced the order accordingly" means a manual quote until one is built.

The operational note is correct and verified: signatures bind version plus a SHA-256 of the exact body (src\lib\contract.ts:184, :349-363), so this needs a new contract_versions row for both locales and re-signature by existing drivers, not an edit in place.
defects: 4.6 anchors the ceiling on "the waiting time stated in the order", but no order in this system states one. Bookings carry stops and, on a round trip, a return time (src\lib\booking.ts:132-135); the pricing engine takes extraStops as a count and nights, with no waiting-duration field anywhere (src\lib\pricing\engine.ts:198-204). The express release — "not obliged to continue waiting after the time stated in the order has expired" — therefore has no trigger in the ordinary case, so the strongest of the three boundedness devices is inoperative exactly where it is needed. Peg the cap to the stops listed and the return time stated (returnAt), and give a default per-stop allowance where the order states none.

Direct contradiction with the customer-facing copy the rationale relies on: src\lib\i18n\en.ts:212 (faq.a3) tells travellers stops "are not time-limited and are not charged extra". 4.6 makes waiting time-limited on the driver side. The clause closes Sandro's gap and opens the mirror-image one — the traveller is promised no time limit while the driver is contractually free to leave. Either amend that FAQ line (and its ka/ru counterparts) or state a default per-stop allowance in 4.6 so the two sides match.

4.6 conditions additional waiting on the Company having "repriced the order accordingly", but there is no waiting or hourly price component to reprice with: engine.ts prices only distance, deadhead, driving time, per-stop fee and overnights, and DECISIONS.md records "Hourly hire is an inquiry, not a price — there are no per-hour rates in driver price plans yet". The clause is contractually valid under 6.1's "agreed commercial terms", but until a wait price exists it commits the Company to a manual quote while a driver waits on the phone. Either build a wait line or soften to "agreed and priced by the Company".

4.7 opens "In accordance with clause 6.6" while going beyond 6.6 in two ways: it forbids accepting as well as demanding, and it removes 6.6's "additional services determined in advance by the Company" exception for waiting and the return. A substantive extension presented as a restatement invites the argument that 6.6 governs and 4.7 adds nothing. Use "Without prejudice to clause 6.6" or "Notwithstanding clause 6.6" and let the wider rule stand openly.

Referent drift: 6.6 and Article 5 impose the no-extra-money rule towards "a customer" / "მომხმარებელი"; 4.7 imposes it towards "the passenger" / "მგზავრი". Where the booker is not the traveller these are different people, so the agreement now states the same prohibition against two different addressees. The passenger framing is the more useful one (cash in the car), but say so deliberately rather than by drift — or align both.

4.5 states that "The price of such an order is determined under clause 6.1 with the return distance included", attributing to 6.1 a rule 6.1 does not contain — 6.1 says only that price is determined in the Company's system or agreed commercial terms. As a driver-facing assurance it is welcome; as drafting it makes the contract text depend on an engine behaviour no clause secures, so a future pricing change could falsify Article 4 without anyone editing the contract. Either put the rule in Article 6 or phrase it as a Company undertaking.

Minor contractor-status friction in 4.6: "such additional waiting is performed only where the Company has agreed it" reads as forbidding the driver to wait longer of his own accord, even for nothing. Recast as a release rather than a restriction — "the Partner Driver is not obliged to perform additional waiting unless the Company has agreed it and repriced the order" — and leave 4.7 to do the anti-side-deal work.

Scope note, not a flaw in the clause: the customer terms (src\lib\legal.ts) say nothing about waiting at stops or a same-day return either — only the marketing copy does. Fixing the driver side alone leaves the promise unenforceable in the other direction; the passenger terms should carry the matching term.

scores.verdict: The Georgian is correct, formal legal Georgian and says substantively the same thing as the English — same obligations, same limits, same escape routes, no divergence that could let a driver who signed the Georgian version be bound differently from one who signed the English. Verb morphology is sound (ვალდებულია + optative დააბრუნოს/განაგრძოს, matching existing 4.3's ვალდებულია გამოცხადდეს), case government is correct throughout (წარმოადგენს ... ნაწილს, მოიცავს ... ლოდინსა და ... მგზავრობას, ვრცელდება ... -ზე, მოსთხოვოს with the correct objective-version marker), and the terms of art are used exactly as the surrounding text uses them (პარტნიორი მძღოლი, კომპანია, დადასტურებული შეკვეთა, and 4.7's პარტნიორ მძღოლს არ აქვს უფლება deliberately mirroring the existing 6.6 construction). Contractor status is preserved on the Georgian side too: ვალდებულია attaches only to the scope of an order already accepted, nothing directs the driver's conduct at the destination, and the closing sentence sends the reader back to 4.2, consistent with 1.4's დამოუკიდებლად მართავს. Boundedness is fully carried in Georgian by all three of the English mechanisms. The remaining defects are syntactic and lexical polish, not meaning: one genuinely misattached relative clause in 4.7, one clumsy comparative construction in 4.6, and a passenger-centric noun (მგზავრობა) used for a driver-side obligation. None of these changes what the driver is bound to, but the 4.7 slip is the kind of thing a Georgian lawyer would strike in a document that is actually signed, so I would fix it before creating the new contract version.
defects: 4.7, misattached relative clause (the one real grammatical error): "შეკვეთის მიღება, რომელიც ითვალისწინებს ლოდინს..." — რომელიც is nominative, but the only nominative head available is მიღება (the acceptance); შეკვეთის is genitive and cannot license it. As written it reads "the acceptance, which provides for waiting", not "an order that provides for waiting". The English is unambiguous ("an order that provides for waiting"). Fix: "ისეთი შეკვეთის მიღება, რომელიც ითვალისწინებს..." (or იმ შეკვეთის).

4.6, broken parallelism in the ceiling sentence: "ვრცელდება მხოლოდ ... გაჩერებებსა და ლოდინის დროზე და არა უფრო ფართო ფარგლებში". The verb ვრცელდება governs -ზე in the first conjunct and is then handed a locative ფარგლებში in the second, so the two halves do not hang off the verb the same way. Meaning survives, but it is not clean legal Georgian for "and to no greater extent". Fix: "...ლოდინის დროზე და არა უფრო ფართოდ", or "...დროზე და არ ვრცელდება ამის მიღმა".

Lexical register, three occurrences: "დაბრუნების მგზავრობა" for "the return journey". მგზავრობა denotes travelling as a passenger (cf. მგზავრობის ღირებულება, and the School body's "ექსკურსიის/მგზავრობის"), so it describes what the passenger does, while the clause is defining what the driver is obliged to perform. დაბრუნების რეისი or უკან დაბრუნების მარშრუტი would sit better beside 4.3's მარშრუტი. Not a divergence — the obligation is identifiable either way.

4.6, dangling object on დათანხმდა: "თუ კომპანია დათანხმდა და შესაბამისად გადაანგარიშა შეკვეთის ღირებულება". The English "has agreed it" has an explicit object; the Georgian დათანხმდა is left without one and has to borrow it from the following conjunct. Cleaner: "თუ კომპანია დაეთანხმა დამატებით ლოდინს და შესაბამისად გადაანგარიშა შეკვეთის ღირებულება".

4.5, small under-specification against the English: "the remuneration payable to the Partner Driver under Article 6" becomes "მე-6 მუხლით გათვალისწინებული ანაზღაურება", dropping "payable to the Partner Driver". Immaterial in effect (Article 6 remuneration is the driver's by definition), but the Georgian states the driver's own payment guarantee slightly less directly than the English does. Suggest "პარტნიორი მძღოლისთვის მე-6 მუხლით გათვალისწინებული ანაზღაურება".

Cross-reference nomenclature (house-style inconsistency the draft inherits rather than creates): the draft writes "6.1. მუხლის", "6.6. მუხლის", "4.2. მუხლის" for sub-clauses. Existing 3.3 calls a sub-clause a პუნქტი ("ამ მუხლის 3.2. პუნქტით"), which is the technically correct Georgian, while 6.5 calls one a მუხლი ("2.1.7. მუხლით"). The draft follows 6.5, so it is defensible, but it produces one sentence in 4.5 carrying მუხლი in both senses at once ("6.1. მუხლის" = sub-clause, "მე-6 მუხლით" = Article). Using პუნქტი for the sub-clause would remove the ambiguity.

Not a KA/EN divergence, but flagged because it affects whether the Georgian cross-reference actually holds: 4.7 grounds itself in 6.6, yet 6.6 prohibits demanding extra sums from the მომხმარებელი (customer) while 4.7 prohibits it as against the მგზავრი (passenger). These are not always the same person (school and corporate bookings especially). The English drafting has the identical gap ("customer" in 6.6, "passenger" in 4.7), so neither version is worse than the other, but 4.7's "წინამდებარე ხელშეკრულების 6.6. მუხლის შესაბამისად" presents as derived a prohibition that is in fact slightly wider than its source. Either widen 6.6 to მომხმარებლისაგან ან მგზავრისგან, or soften 4.7's opening to "წინამდებარე ხელშეკრულების 6.6. პუნქტის გათვალისწინებით" — in both languages simultaneously.

scores.verdict: Sound on both questions the brief puts, with one real overstatement. RETURN-LEG ECONOMICS: accurate, and carefully scoped. `directions = roundTrip ? 2n : 1n` (src/lib/pricing/engine.ts:147) bills distance both ways and doubles driving minutes (engine.ts:167, 190), and `deadheadFull = roundTrip ? 0n : ...` (engine.ts:178) removes the empty-return line because the driver comes home loaded — exactly what DECISIONS.md records. So 4.5's "the remuneration payable under Article 6 covers ... that return journey" is a true statement, not a request for unpaid work. The drafter also avoided the trap of overclaiming on one-ways: the one-way return is only PARTIALLY paid (applyBps(deadheadFull, deadheadRecoveryBps), engine.ts:179 — a configured recovery share, not the full leg), and 4.5's pricing sentence is confined to orders providing a same-day return, so it never asserts something the engine does not do. ROADSIDE SETTLEMENT: correctly forbidden and correctly routed. 4.7 forbids the driver to "request or to accept" — a deliberate strengthening of 6.6, which forbids only demanding — and 4.6 sends extra waiting to the Company for agreement and repricing with settlement under Article 6, which closes 6.6's own carve-out ("other than for additional services determined in advance by the Company") that would otherwise have let a driver take cash for Company-approved extra waiting. That keeps the money flow consistent with 6.5 and with Article 5, which already treats side-deals as a breach. CONTRACTOR STATUS: preserved. The duty is framed as the scope of an order already accepted rather than as an instruction about the driver's time, nothing directs his conduct at the destination, and 4.7's closing sentence points back to 4.2, consistent with 1.4 (db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:247/431). BILINGUAL PARITY: I compared clause by clause and found no divergence of meaning. The operational note is right too: src/lib/contract.ts:184/334/351 binds a SHA-256 of the resolved body to each signature, so this needs a new version row, not an edit. WHERE IT FALLS SHORT: 4.5 claims the Article 6 remuneration covers "that waiting" as well as the return. For the return that is demonstrable; for the waiting it is a deeming provision with no pricing input behind it, and the gap sits precisely in the case the clause makes binding — a same-day wait-and-return. There is no waiting line item in the engine's QuoteLine union, the day floor is switched off for it (`bookedDays = tour || nights > 0 ? nights + 1 : 0`, src/lib/offers.ts:301, and QuoteInputs.days documents that a transfer "is priced by distance and the day floor never applies to it"), yet roundTripWindow (offers.ts:111-116) blocks the driver's calendar from pickup to return plus the drive home. A 30-minute wait and a 7-hour wait produce an identical quote while both consume the day. The driver is not trapped — 4.2 keeps acceptance voluntary and 4.6 bounds the duty — but a driver who checks the arithmetic will find the clause's own economic justification is only half-earned, which is the one thing a clause written to answer Sandro cannot afford. Boundedness is also uneven: it genuinely bites for wait-and-return because the order carries `returnAt`, but for waiting at stops the system stores only a stop COUNT (`extraStops`), so "the waiting time stated in the order" and the release "after the time stated in the order has expired" have no referent for the case the site advertises as "Waiting at them is not charged extra". Net: publishable after the 4.5 wording is trimmed to what the engine actually pays for, and after a stated waiting allowance per stop exists to give 4.6 something to bound.
defects: 4.5 overstates its own economic justification: it says the Article 6 remuneration covers 'that waiting' as well as the return, but no waiting time is priced anywhere. src/lib/pricing/engine.ts has no waiting line in its QuoteLine union, and for a same-day round trip the day floor is disabled (bookedDays = tour || nights > 0 ? nights + 1 : 0, src/lib/offers.ts:301; QuoteInputs.days states the day floor 'never applies' to a transfer). A 30-minute and a 7-hour wait yield an identical quote, while roundTripWindow (src/lib/offers.ts:111-116) blocks the driver's calendar for the whole span. The return-journey half of the sentence is backed by the engine; the waiting half is a deeming provision the driver can disprove.

4.6's ceiling is inoperative for waiting at stops on a one-way. The booking captures returnAt for round trips, so the ceiling and the release both bite there, but for stops the model stores only a count (extraStops, src/lib/pricing/engine.ts) with no per-stop waiting duration anywhere. 'the waiting time stated in the order' and 'after the time stated in the order has expired' therefore have no referent in exactly the case the site advertises ('Waiting at them is not charged extra', src/lib/i18n/en.ts:194), leaving waiting at a listed stop bounded in which stops but not in how long.

4.6 promises a repricing route the platform does not have. There is no per-booking amendment or repricing path: the only repricing in the codebase is a marketplace-wide band change (src/app/admin/actions.ts:824-830), and src/app/admin/pricing/page.tsx:96 states that bookings already made keep their own quote. Since 4.6's Company-agreed repricing is the mechanism that makes 4.7's prohibition fair, a driver who waits beyond the order today gets nothing and is contractually barred from taking cash.

Scope gap on multi-day round trips. 4.5 attaches the return obligation only 'where the order provides for a return on the same day', but src/lib/offers.ts:192-199 prices any returnAt after departure and counts nights across calendar boundaries, so an overnight round trip is a sellable product with no driver-side return duty — while 'The driver stays with you and brings you back' (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:607) is shown for round trips generally. The brief specified same-day, so this is the brief's boundary as much as the drafter's, but it should be raised rather than silently inherited.

4.7 is keyed to 'the passenger' / 'მგზავრს' while the clause it invokes, 6.6, and the side-deal prohibition in Article 5 are keyed to 'a customer' / 'მომხმარებელი'. A booking can be made by someone other than the rider (a hotel or agency), so the prohibition 4.7 draws is narrower than the one it claims to be applying, and money taken from the booker rather than the rider sits outside its literal terms in both languages.

4.5's 'The price of such an order is determined under clause 6.1 with the return distance included' attributes a substantive pricing rule to 6.1, which says only that the price is determined in the Company's system or in the agreed commercial terms (db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql). The statement is true of the engine for roundTrip orders and is driver-favourable, but it is an addition to 6.1 rather than an application of it; the cross-reference reads as if 6.1 already contains the rule.

scores.verdict: Competent drafting that correctly identifies and partly closes a real one-directional gap, with genuine strengths — waiting is attached to the existing 4.3 obligation rather than bolted on as a new one, "forms part of the same order and does not constitute a new order" forecloses roadside renegotiation, repricing is routed through the Company consistently with 5.2/6.5/6.6, contractor status is properly preserved via the 4.2 pointer that matches 1.4, and the Georgian and English say the same thing in the right register. But both sides find real holes. The driver's lawyer defeats the waiting obligation entirely: 4.6 caps the duty at "the waiting time stated in the order", and no wait duration exists anywhere in the system — booking_legs carries position/label/day_index/notes, the engine charges a per-stop count with no duration, and the itinerary stores bare stop labels — so the ceiling is a ceiling on an empty set and a ninety-second stop is literal compliance, defeating the very "waiting is not charged extra" promise the clause exists to answer. The passenger's lawyer finds two more: "same day" excludes multi-day round trips, a product the engine explicitly prices with overnight fees and the site promises "brings you back" without qualification; and the 4.6 release lets a driver leave at 17:01 on a 17:00 return with no grace period, no duty to notify the Company before abandoning the passenger, and no forfeiture of the return-leg fee 4.5 says he was already paid. Two further defects cut against the driver: 4.7 is presented as declaratory of 6.6 while actually widening it from "demand" to "demand or accept" (catching unsolicited tips, under 5.3's deactivation machinery), and 4.5's economic reassurance cross-references 6.1, which fixes no pricing method at all. Fixable by targeted edits rather than a rewrite, but as written the waiting limb — the core of the brief — does not bind.
defects: Fatal to requirement (a): 4.6 limits the waiting duty to "the waiting time stated in the order", but no wait-duration field exists anywhere in the system — booking_legs (db/migrations/0002_booking_money_comms.sql) carries only position/label/day_index/notes, src/lib/pricing/engine.ts:199 charges extraStops x perStopFeeMinor (a count, no duration), and the itinerary JSONB carries stops as bare string labels. A driver's lawyer reads the ceiling literally: no waiting time is stated, therefore the obligation extends to none. Stop, wait ninety seconds, drive on — full compliance with the words, and the en.ts:194 promise "Waiting at them is not charged extra" is left with no counterpart. The clause pegs its ceiling to a datum the order does not carry and supplies no default (no "reasonable", no minimum, nothing).

"Return on the same day" excludes multi-day round trips, which are a real and priced product: src/components/search-form.tsx:98 accepts any return later than departure with no same-day cap, console.overnightHint reads "Your accommodation and meals on multi-day trips", and DECISIONS.md charges overnights when the return crosses a calendar day. The 4.5 return obligation therefore does not attach at all to a two-day round trip, while search.roundTripNote ("The driver stays with you and brings you back") is displayed unqualified for every round trip. The engine's overnight line is direct evidence the commercial reality is wider than the clause.

The 4.6 release is absolute with no grace and no forfeiture: on a 17:00 stated return the driver "is not obliged to continue waiting after the time stated in the order has expired" from 17:01, and nothing conditions the Article 6 remuneration — which 4.5 states already covers the return journey — on actually carrying the passenger back. The driver may lawfully leave a passenger stranded and keep the return-leg fee. Note the asymmetry: 4.6 imposes a duty to notify the Company before additional waiting, but imposes none before departing without the passenger; clause 7.6 covers only lateness to an order, not early abandonment of one.

4.7 is mislabelled as declaratory. It opens "In accordance with clause 6.6", and the rationale claims it "does not invent a new prohibition", but 6.6 bars only demanding ("is not entitled to demand" / "არ აქვს უფლება, მომხმარებლისგან მოითხოვოს") whereas 4.7 bars requesting OR accepting ("or to accept" / "ან მისგან მიიღოს"). This constitutively widens the ban to cover unsolicited tips for long waits, exposing the driver to Article 5.3 warning, suspension or deactivation, while the framing invites him to read it as restating a rule that permits what he did not demand.

4.5's economic reassurance is asserted rather than secured: it states the price "is determined under clause 6.1 with the return distance included", but 6.1 provides only that price is "determined in the Company's system or in the agreed commercial terms" — no method, no distance, no return leg, and unilaterally variable by the Company. The rationale's claim that "the driver can read the economic justification inside the clause that binds him" is not delivered by the cross-reference actually used.

Referent inconsistency in 4.7: it prohibits taking additional sums from "the passenger" / "მგზავრს", whereas 6.6 prohibits taking them from "a customer" / "მომხმარებლისგან". The agreement distinguishes the two (5.1, 5.2 and 6.6 use customer; 7.3–7.5 use passenger), and a booker such as a hotel is not the rider, so 4.7's own words do not reach extra money taken from the booker. 4.7 also drops 6.6's carve-out for "additional services determined in advance by the Company", so a Company-defined paid waiting service would flatly contradict 4.7.

en:
4.5. Waiting at the stops stated in a confirmed order, and waiting while the passenger is at a destination from which the order provides for a same-day return, form part of performing the agreed route; where the order provides for a same-day return, the Partner Driver is obliged to carry the passenger back under the same order. Such waiting and such return carriage are covered by the price of that order, and the Partner Driver is not obliged to wait beyond the extent stated in the order.

4.6. The Partner Driver is not entitled to demand any sum from a passenger for such waiting or for the return carriage. Waiting beyond the extent stated in the order is agreed with the Company, which determines the price of the order accordingly; it is not settled with the passenger.
