rationale:
Two paragraphs, split along the two things a driver could otherwise argue about: what he owes (4.5) and who he may ask for money (4.6).

4.5 does the binding. It states that waiting at the order's stops and waiting while the passenger is at the destination is part of performing the agreed route — i.e. it hangs off the obligation already created in 4.3 ("perform the route agreed with the Company") rather than creating a new free-standing duty, which keeps it a description of the contracted service and not an employment-style instruction about how the driver spends his day. The same-day return is written as part of the same order, which is what the pricing engine assumes: a round trip counts distance in both directions, and a one-way already includes the deadhead return, so in both cases the fee the driver receives has already paid for the return journey. Saying "covered by the price of that order" writes that down; it does not ask for unpaid work.

4.6 closes the customer-facing hole. Article 6.6 already forbids demanding extra sums from a customer, but a driver could read waiting as outside the order altogether and therefore outside 6.6; 4.6 names waiting and the return specifically and routes any extra waiting to the Company, which reprices it. That keeps money off the roadside and inside the system, which is also what 5.2 (no bypassing the Company's system) is protecting.

Terminology follows the existing text exactly: "the Partner Driver"/"პარტნიორი მძღოლი", "a confirmed order"/"დადასტურებული შეკვეთა", "is obliged to"/"ვალდებულია", "the Company"/"კომპანია", and "passenger"/"მგზავრი" for the person in the car (the agreement uses "customer"/"მომხმარებელი" for the booking party in Articles 5 and 6, so 4.6 says "passenger" for the person who might be asked for cash). Both versions carry the same four propositions in the same order and the same numbering.

Note for whoever applies this: the driver agreement lives in C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\db\migrations\0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql — Georgian Article 4 at lines 285-293, English at lines 469-477. That migration may already have been applied, so the new clauses should go into a fresh migration and a contract version bump rather than an edit in place.
boundedness:
The obligation is capped three times over, all inside 4.5-4.6 and all tied to the order document rather than to the passenger's wishes.

1. The duty attaches only to waiting "at the stops stated in a confirmed order" and to a destination "from which the order provides for a same-day return". No stop in the order, no duty. No same-day return in the order, no duty to wait at the destination and no duty to carry back.

2. An express ceiling: "the Partner Driver is not obliged to wait beyond the extent stated in the order" / "არ არის ვალდებული ელოდოს შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ფარგლებს გარეთ". The cap is stated as a right of refusal, so a driver reading only 4.5 sees his own limit in the same sentence as his obligation.

3. Extra waiting is a new agreement, not an extension of the old one: it "is agreed with the Company, which determines the price of the order accordingly". Two consequences — the driver can say no, since agreement is required; and if he says yes, the fee moves. Nothing lets waiting grow at constant pay.

The passenger has no power to enlarge the obligation at any point: everything runs through what the order states or what the Company subsequently agrees, and 4.6 removes the roadside negotiation that would otherwise be the informal route to open-endedness.

scores.verdict: ADOPT WITH AMENDMENTS — 7.5/10 as contract drafting. The clause is well-made where the task set the bar: numbering (4.5, 4.6 appended after 4.4 — correct not to renumber an executed instrument), register and vocabulary all match (`the Partner Driver`/`პარტნიორი მძღოლი`, `a confirmed order`/`დადასტურებული შეკვეთა`, `is obliged to`/`ვალდებულია`, `carriage`/`carrying` is already house usage at 9.2 and 11.5; `მგზავრი` for the person in the car vs `მომხმარებელი` at 5.2/6.6 for the booking party is a real distinction in the existing text, verified at db/migrations/0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:299,315,363, and the drafter read it correctly). No conflict with 4.2: the duty attaches only to `a confirmed order`, i.e. after the accept/decline decision, so it defines what is being accepted rather than overriding the right to decline. No conflict with 4.3: hanging the waiting on "form part of performing the agreed route" rather than creating a free-standing duty is the single best decision in the draft — it keeps the clause a description of the contracted deliverable, so nothing here reads as an instruction to a subordinate and Articles 1.3/1.4 survive intact. The independent-contractor characterisation is not undermined by the framing.\n\nWhat pulls the score down is that the bound is only as good as the term it points at, and "the extent stated in the order" is undefined in the instrument and largely non-existent in the order the driver actually sees. Both branches of 4.5 lean on it, and it holds for the same-day return (the itinerary carries `returnAt`) but is empty for stops (recorded as slugs only) and is never surfaced on the driver's order card at all. So on paper the obligation is capped three times as the rationale claims; in operation a driver acknowledges an order without being shown the return time or even whether it is a round trip, and the engine prices no waiting duration for a transfer. The clause is sound but should not go into a new migration until defects 1-3 and 6 are addressed; 4, 5, 7 are one-line textual fixes worth taking at the same time.
defects: THE CAP POINTS AT A TERM THAT DOES NOT EXIST IN THE ORDER THE DRIVER SEES. The entire ceiling is 'the extent stated in the order' / 'შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ფარგლებს', but the agreement nowhere says what an order must state about waiting, and the system does not state it. The itinerary carries returnAt (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\offers.ts:206-212), which feeds only the availability tstzrange (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\booking.ts:213-214); `bookings` stores `service_start_at` and no end column (no `service_end_at` exists anywhere in src or db/migrations); and the driver's order query selects service_start_at, drive_minutes, legs and addresses and neither the return time nor a round-trip flag (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\app\driver\orders\page.tsx:35-47). The driver is therefore bound at acknowledgement to an extent he was never shown. FIX: define the term in 4.5 ('the waiting time and the return time stated in the order' / 'შეკვეთით მითითებული ლოდინის დრო და დაბრუნების დრო') and surface the return time on the order card before the driver acknowledges.

THE FIRST BRANCH OF 4.5 IS UNCAPPED IN SUBSTANCE. Waiting 'at the stops stated in a confirmed order' is bounded by the same 'extent stated in the order', but an order records stops as slugs only and the engine charges a flat perStopFeeMinor per stop irrespective of duration (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\pricing\engine.ts, step 4). No duration is ever stated for a stop, so the ceiling has no content there: a passenger argues the stop is named without limit, a driver argues no extent is stated so nothing is owed. Either reading defeats the clause's purpose. FIX: add a default in the clause itself — waiting at a stop for which the order states no duration does not exceed a stated number of minutes.

'COVERED BY THE PRICE OF THAT ORDER' IS TRUE OF THE RETURN AND NOT TRUE OF THE WAITING. The rationale is right that the return journey is already paid (roundTrip doubles distance and time; a one-way recovers deadhead), but the engine has no line item that varies with waiting duration: time = directions x driveMinutes x ratePerMinute, and the per-day floor applies only when days > 0, which is set from tour.duration_days only (C:\Users\user\Claude\RoutePlanner\src\lib\pricing\engine.ts:231-238 and src\lib\offers.ts:211). A round-trip transfer whose passenger stays nine hours prices identically to one whose passenger stays one hour. 4.5 makes that wait contractually binding while the fee is blind to it, so the rationale's claim that 'nothing lets waiting grow at constant pay' holds only at the extension step (4.6), not at acceptance. This is also where the independent-contractor risk actually sits: an unpriced, unbounded requirement to remain at the customer's disposal is what an inspector reads as working time, and it sits directly against 1.4 / 'სამუშაო გრაფიკს'.

4.6 CONTRADICTS 6.6 WITH NO STATED PRIORITY. 6.6 permits demanding additional sums from a customer 'for additional services determined in advance by the Company'; 4.6 forbids any sum for waiting or the return with no saving. If the Company ever designates extended waiting as a priced add-on collected in the car, the two clauses give opposite answers and nothing resolves which governs. FIX: open 4.6 with 'Notwithstanding clause 6.6' / 'ამ ხელშეკრულების 6.6 პუნქტის მიუხედავად', or carve the 6.6 exception in expressly.

PERSON GAP IN 4.6. It binds only as to 'a passenger' / 'მგზავრს'. The word choice is correct for the person in the car, but the clause's own justification is that a driver may read waiting as falling outside 6.6 altogether — and if it does, a demand for waiting money addressed to the booking customer (a company, a school, a parent not travelling; 'მომხმარებელი' in 5.2 and 6.6) escapes both 4.6 and 6.6. FIX: 'from a passenger or customer' / 'მგზავრს ან მომხმარებელს'.

NO PROCEDURE WHEN THE EXTENT EXPIRES. 4.5 gives the driver a right to stop waiting but the agreement says nothing about what he then does. 4.3's notification duty runs to 'any delay, accident, technical problem or other emergency circumstance', which does not naturally cover a passenger who simply has not returned. A driver who exercises his 4.5 right and departs is exposed under 11.7 (customer complaints, grounds for reviewing status) and 9.1. This is the exact scenario the clause exists to govern, and it is the one it leaves unwritten. FIX: add to 4.5 or as 4.7 — where the passenger does not appear within the extent stated, the Partner Driver notifies the Company without delay and acts on its instruction.

KA/EN DIVERGENCE IN THE SECOND BRANCH OF 4.5, ON THE GOVERNING TEXT. English ties the wait to 'a destination FROM WHICH the order provides for a same-day return'. The Georgian drops the link: 'ლოდინი მგზავრის დანიშნულების ადგილზე ყოფნის განმავლობაში, როდესაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას' conditions it on the order providing a same-day return at all. On a multi-destination itinerary (stops[] plus destination) the Georgian — which the preamble makes governing — makes waiting at any destination part of the route, while the English confines it to the one the return runs from. FIX: 'ლოდინი მგზავრის იმ დანიშნულების ადგილზე ყოფნის განმავლობაში, საიდანაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას'.

MINOR — 'covered by the price of that order' / 'ამავე შეკვეთის ღირებულებით' is ambiguous between the gross customer price and the driver's share, which 6.2 splits by commission. Since the whole point of the sentence is to tell the driver he has already been paid, tie it to Article 6: 'is remunerated within the driver's share of that order determined under Article 6' / '...მე-6 მუხლით განსაზღვრული მძღოლის წილის ფარგლებში'.

scores.verdict: The Georgian is correct, formal legal Georgian and is substantively faithful: verb morphology, case endings and terms of art are right, the constructions mirror existing clauses (4.3's "ვალდებულია + aorist subjunctive", 6.6's "არ აქვს უფლება, ...", 6.1's "შეკვეთის ღირებულება", the file's own "ფარგლებს გარეთ" idiom at lines 377/738), the მგზავრი/მომხმარებელი distinction is handled as intended, and all four propositions plus all three limits appear in the same order and numbering as the English. It also matches the public site's Georgian vocabulary exactly (გაჩერებები/ლოდინი, დაგელოდება და უკან დაგაბრუნებს). It falls short of a clean pass on one point: the same-day-return condition is rendered as a comma-delimited "როდესაც" clause sitting immediately before the main verb, which can attach to the whole compound subject rather than only to the destination limb — a reading the English relative clause "from which the order provides for a same-day return" forecloses. Under the loose Georgian reading, waiting at planned stops on a plain one-way falls outside 4.5, i.e. precisely the case the site promises is included. Fix by adopting the file's own restrictive pattern (ისეთ ... საიდანაც, cf. lines 704 and 744). Remaining points are register-level, not fidelity-breaking.
defects: ATTACHMENT AMBIGUITY (the one real divergence, 4.5): in '... გაჩერებებზე ლოდინი, ისევე როგორც ლოდინი მგზავრის დანიშნულების ადგილზე ყოფნის განმავლობაში, როდესაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას, წარმოადგენს ...' the comma-delimited როდესაც clause sits directly before the main verb and can be read as qualifying the entire compound subject, not just the second limb. That reading confines the whole waiting duty to same-day-return orders and leaves a one-way with planned stops uncovered — contradicting the site promise at src/lib/i18n/ka.ts:36 and :70 ('დაგეგმილი გაჩერებები და ლოდინი ფასში შედის'). The English 'a destination from which the order provides for a same-day return' is a relative clause locked to the destination and cannot detach. Fix using the document's own restrictive construction (0015_contracts_v2_and_schools.sql:704, :744): '... ისევე როგორც ლოდინი მგზავრის ისეთ დანიშნულების ადგილზე ყოფნის განმავლობაში, საიდანაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას, წარმოადგენს ...'

REGISTER (4.6): 'შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულზე მეტი ლოდინი თანხმდება კომპანიასთან' — the preverbless present of თანხმობა with an inanimate subject reads oddly; the intended passive-general sense is better carried by 'შეთანხმდება კომპანიასთან' or, in the register the document uses elsewhere, 'ექვემდებარება კომპანიასთან შეთანხმებას' / 'საჭიროებს კომპანიასთან წინასწარ შეთანხმებას'. The neighbouring 'წესრიგდება' makes the present-passive rhythm defensible, so this is style, not grammar.

AMBIGUOUS REFERENT: bare 'დაბრუნება' in the second sentence of 4.5 ('აღნიშნული ლოდინი და დაბრუნება') and in 4.6 ('აღნიშნული ლოდინის ან დაბრუნებისთვის') can denote the driver's own return rather than carrying the passenger back — and the driver's empty return leg is a live, separately priced concept in this very contract's commercial model (deadhead, src/lib/pricing/engine.ts). The English pins it as 'return carriage'. 'აღნიშნული' carries the anaphora so it works, but 'მგზავრის უკან დაბრუნება' would remove the doubt.

LEXICAL DRIFT (cosmetic): the English says 'stated in the order' in both 4.5 and 4.6; the Georgian uses 'მითითებულ' for the stops but 'შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ(ზე)' for the extent of waiting. Internally consistent and arguably stronger (განისაზღვრება is the file's own verb for order pricing, clause 6.1), so it does not weaken the cap, but it is not a word-for-word match.

PARALLELISM NIT (4.6): 'მგზავრს მოსთხოვოს რაიმე თანხა' switches verb frame relative to the model clause 6.6 ('მომხმარებლისგან მოითხოვოს დამატებითი თანხა'). Both are correct Georgian and the person switch (მგზავრი, not მომხმარებელი) is deliberate and right; using 'მგზავრისგან მოითხოვოს' would make the deliberate parallel to 6.6 visible on the page.

NOT A GEORGIAN DEFECT, shared by both versions: the pricing engine's roundTrip flag is paired with a return date and time (src/lib/i18n/ka.ts:586 'დაბრუნების თარიღი და დრო') that need not be the same day, yet both 4.5 and its English twin scope the duty to 'იმავე დღეს დაბრუნება' / 'same-day return'. A booked overnight round trip falls outside the clause in both languages equally.

scores.verdict: Directionally right and well-drafted, but not yet shippable. The clause is contractor-safe (it hangs the duty off 4.3's existing "perform the route agreed with the Company" rather than creating an employment-style instruction about the driver's day), it is correct on the round-trip economics, and 4.6 correctly forbids roadside settlement and routes extra waiting to the Company, closing the gap where a driver could read waiting as outside 6.6. Bilingual parity and terminology are good: "მგზავრი" matches Articles 7.3-7.5, "ლოდინი" matches the Georgian customer-facing copy, and both versions carry the same four propositions in the same order. Two substantive defects block it. First, the stop-waiting limb binds the driver to a duration the order cannot state and pays him a fee that is zero by default — precisely the "unpaid cost" the brief forbade. Second, "same-day return" is narrower than what the system actually sells: offers.ts sets roundTrip on any return after departure including multi-day stays, charges overnight fees, and blocks the driver's calendar for the whole stay, so the highest-value wait-and-return bookings fall outside the trigger and the original hole stays open there. Fix those two and this is good; as it stands it half-closes the gap Sandro raised while opening a new one against the driver.
defects: Stop waiting is uncapped in fact and uncompensated by default, so the clause does impose a cost the driver is not paid for. There is no dwell/wait/stop-duration field anywhere in the codebase: stops reach the engine only as `extraStops` (a count) multiplied by `per_stop_fee_minor`, which is `DEFAULT 0` in db/migrations/0001_baseline.sql:281 and is set by the driver himself (src/app/driver/actions.ts:354). The detour's distance and time are paid because stops become routing waypoints (src/lib/offers.ts:180), but the standing time is not. So 4.5's ceiling — 'not obliged to wait beyond the extent stated in the order' / 'შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ფარგლებს გარეთ' — has nothing to attach to for stops, while the public copy promises unlimited free waiting at them in all three languages (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:42, 77, 194 and the ka/ru equivalents). Either reading is bad: if the extent is nil the driver owes no waiting at all and the clause fails its purpose, or the extent is implied and he is bound to unbounded standing time against a possibly-zero fee. Fix: add a per-stop waiting allowance to the itinerary and the quote inputs and have 4.5 refer to it, or word the cap as a stated minimum ('not less than the waiting stated in the order').

The 'same-day return' trigger is narrower than the commercial reality the engine prices. src/lib/offers.ts:192 sets `roundTrip` on ANY return later than departure, not same-day ones only; offers.ts:195-199 then computes `nights` from the calendar day boundaries the stay crosses and charges `overnightFeeMinor`, and `roundTripWindow` (offers.ts:111, with the comment 'A round trip blocks the driver for the entire journey — out, the stay, and the drive home') blocks the driver's calendar for the whole stay. On a two- or three-day wait-and-return the driver is therefore paid for both loaded directions plus overnight, yet 4.5's condition ('a destination from which the order provides for a same-day return' / 'როდესაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას') is not met, so he owes neither the waiting nor the return carriage. That is the exact hole the clause was written to close, left open on the largest bookings. Fix: say 'where the order provides for a return journey' / 'დაბრუნებას' and let the extent cap do the limiting work, since returnAt already bounds it.

4.6's remedy points to a repricing channel that does not exist in the system. No code path anywhere changes `gross_minor` or `driver_net_minor` on a confirmed booking: the admin booking edit updates only pickup_address, dropoff_address, flight_number, pickup_sign_name, customer_phone and notes (src/app/admin/actions.ts:540-557); reassignment changes driver and vehicle (src/lib/operations.ts:158); cancellation writes a fee; and src/app/admin/pricing/page.tsx:96 states that 'Bookings already made keep their own frozen price'. So 4.6 correctly bans settlement with the passenger and then routes the driver to a Company that currently cannot raise the price of his order. Article 6.1 ('or in the agreed commercial terms' / 'შეთანხმებულ კომერციულ პირობებში') gives the clause contractual footing, so it is not incoherent, but it needs either an admin repricing path or a documented settlement-time adjustment before the promise is honest to the driver.

The no-show wait is still uncovered — the same defect Sandro raised, in a second place. The customer terms promise that the driver waits, with a grace period of 30 minutes and longer for tracked airport pickups (src/lib/legal.ts:252, cross-referenced at legal.ts:104). `no_show_grace_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 30` exists at db/migrations/0002_booking_money_comms.sql:323 but is read nowhere in src/, so that extent lives in prose and policy, not in the order. Under 4.5's cap ('the extent stated in the order') a driver can decline to wait for a late passenger at the pickup point, and the Company is again promising customers something no driver has agreed to.

4.5's binding limb and its ceiling are not symmetrical in what they reference, which invites the wrong argument. The obligation is framed on 'the stops stated in a confirmed order', a concept the itinerary really does carry (origin, stops[], destination), whereas the ceiling is framed on 'the extent stated in the order', a concept the order carries only for the destination wait (via returnAt) and not at all for stops. A driver reading only 4.5 sees a duty with a defined scope and an undefined limit. Anchor both to the same field.

'Waiting beyond the extent stated in the order is agreed with the Company, which determines the price of the order accordingly' / 'თანხმდება კომპანიასთან, რომელიც შესაბამისად განსაზღვრავს შეკვეთის ღირებულებას' is internally loose: it requires agreement and then gives the Company the unilateral power to set what that agreement is worth. The rationale's claim that 'if he says yes, the fee moves' is not what the text guarantees — the text guarantees only that the Company will decide. 4.5's refusal right rescues the driver in practice, so this is minor, but 'and the price of the order is adjusted accordingly by agreement' would say what was intended. The looseness is identical in both languages, so it is a drafting point, not a translation one.

Minor bilingual drift on the same-day-return condition. The English attaches it to the place — 'a destination FROM WHICH the order provides for a same-day return' — while the Georgian attaches it to the order at large — 'ლოდინი მგზავრის დანიშნულების ადგილზე ყოფნის განმავლობაში, როდესაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს იმავე დღეს დაბრუნებას'. Immaterial on a single-destination transfer, divergent on a multi-stop order where the return runs from one point but not another. Since a driver may sign either version, tighten the Georgian to 'იმ დანიშნულების ადგილზე, საიდანაც შეკვეთა ითვალისწინებს...'.

Unresolved tension with Article 6.6, which permits demanding additional sums from a customer 'for additional services determined in advance by the Company' / 'გარდა კომპანიის მიერ წინასწარ განსაზღვრული დამატებითი მომსახურებისა'. If the Company ever lists waiting as such a pre-determined additional service, 6.6 permits collection and 4.6 flatly forbids it. Lex specialis probably resolves it in 4.6's favour, but a driver arguing the point has a foothold. Open 4.6 with 'Notwithstanding clause 6.6' / 'ამ ხელშეკრულების 6.6 მუხლის მიუხედავად' so the hierarchy is explicit.

scores.verdict: Competent drafting on the wrong facts. The register, bilingual equivalence and contractor-safety are genuinely good: hanging the duty off 4.3 rather than creating a free-standing one keeps it a description of the contracted service and not an employment instruction, and routing extra waiting through the Company is consistent with 5.2 and 6.6. But both lawyers find real holes, and two of them are fatal to the clause's purpose. (1) The cap "the extent stated in the order" is empty for stops: the order records stop slugs and nothing else — no dwell field exists in the schema, the engine, or the UI — so a driver's lawyer says the stated extent of waiting is nil, my client halted as the order required, and every actual minute of waiting is "beyond the extent stated" and must be repriced by the Company. The cap swallows the obligation in precisely the case the website advertises. (2) "Same-day return" is narrower than the product sold: roundTrip is any returnAt after travelAt, the return input accepts a later date, and multi-night wait-and-return is priced with both directions plus an overnight fee — yet 4.5 imposes no duty to carry the passenger back on an overnight round trip, and by expressly naming same-day returns it weakens the 4.3 argument the Company would otherwise make for the rest. Add unaddressed waiting at pickup, no grace period before the driver may lawfully drive off, and no stated entitlement to extra pay for agreed extra waiting, and the clause does not yet close the gap Sandro identified. Fixable: replace "same-day" with "a return journey", supply a default extent where the order states none (and add the field), extend the duty to the pickup point, and require notification to the Company before departing.
defects: SEVERE - the cap is empty for stops, so 4.5's obligation is self-defeating. The duty is capped by "the extent stated in the order" / "შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ფარგლებს", but an order states no waiting duration at all: the itinerary is {origin, stops: string[], destination} (src/lib/offers.ts:206-211), stops are place slugs, and no dwell/duration field exists in the schema, the pricing engine or the booking UI (extraStops is a bare count at offers.ts:313 times perStopFeeMinor at engine.ts:199). A driver's lawyer therefore argues: the extent of waiting stated in this order is nil; my client stopped at Ananuri as the order required and drove on; every minute of actual waiting is "waiting beyond the extent stated in the order", which under 4.6 must be agreed with the Company and repriced. He can lawfully refuse to wait one minute at any stop and demand a call to the office. That defeats exactly the promise the clause exists to back: "Add stops when you book. Waiting at them is not charged extra." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:194, ka.ts:182). Fix: either the order document must carry a per-stop waiting figure, or 4.5 must supply a default where none is stated (waiting reasonable for the purpose of the stop, and in any event not less than N minutes).

SEVERE - "same-day return" does not match the product. Round trip is defined as any return after departure, with no same-day constraint (src/lib/offers.ts:192); the return field is a datetime-local with min={when} (src/components/search-form.tsx:179 and :263), so a customer books a next-day or three-day return; nights are computed from day boundaries crossed and priced with overnightFeeMinor (offers.ts:196-199). On a Tbilisi-Kazbegi overnight wait-and-return the driver is paid for both loaded directions plus an overnight fee, and 4.5 still imposes no duty to bring the passenger home, because the order does not provide for a SAME-DAY return. The customer-facing promise has no such limit either: "The driver stays with you and brings you back - usually cheaper than two one-way trips" (en.ts:607). Worse, the drafting is affirmatively harmful: by expressly binding only same-day returns it invites expressio unius - naming one class of return implies other returns are outside the agreed route - which weakens the 4.3 argument the Company would otherwise run for multi-day trips. The condition should be "where the order provides for a return journey", full stop.

SERIOUS - waiting at the PICKUP is not covered at all. The duty attaches to "the stops stated in a confirmed order" and to the destination; the origin is neither, and the itinerary model keeps origin, stops and destination as separate fields (offers.ts:206-210). 4.3 only requires the driver to "attend at the stated time and place". A driver who attends at 09:00 and departs at 09:02 because the passenger has not come down from the hotel has complied with 4.3 and is untouched by 4.5 or 4.6. This is the most common real dispute in airport and hotel work, and the home-page promise "Planned stops and waiting are included in the price. You pay nothing extra." (en.ts:42, ka.ts:36) reads to a customer as covering it squarely.

SERIOUS - no grace period and no duty to stay while the Company reprices, so the passenger can be lawfully stranded. The cap is drafted purely as a right of refusal, so the driver may depart the instant the stated extent expires. 4.6 requires extra waiting to be "agreed with the Company", but nothing obliges the driver to notify the Company, or to remain while that agreement is sought, before leaving. 4.3's notification duty is limited to "delay, accident, technical problem or other emergency circumstance", which a driver will say does not describe a passenger who is ten minutes late. Needs a minimum tolerance plus a limb along the lines of "the Partner Driver shall not depart before notifying the Company and receiving its instruction".

MODERATE (driver side) - "agreed with the Company, which determines the price of the order accordingly" gives the driver no entitlement to be paid more. "Determines the price accordingly" is neutral as to direction, and read with 6.1 ("the price of each order is determined in the Company's system") and the fixed split in 6.2, a driver's lawyer sees a unilateral Company determination with no stated waiting rate and no promise of an increase. The rationale's defence ("if he says yes, the fee moves") is not what the words say. It should read that the Company determines the additional remuneration payable for that waiting.

MODERATE - tours and day hire are unaddressed. A tour is expressly excluded from roundTrip (`!tour`, offers.ts:192) and priced by days against minimumDayFareMinor, with the driver waiting all day while passengers hike or eat. Those waits are neither stops in the transfer sense nor a same-day-return destination wait, so 4.5 gives them no anchor and no stated extent. The same gap applies to multi-day hire (`days`/`nights` in QuoteInputs).

MINOR - 4.6 binds only as against "a passenger" / "მგზავრი", but the booking party is often not in the car: a school (school agreement Article 9 and the Annex 1 order sheets in this same migration), a hotel, an agency. A driver who invoices the school for waiting is outside 4.6 by its own terms and falls back on 6.6, which itself permits sums "for additional services determined in advance by the Company" - leaving a seam to argue extended waiting is such a service and collect it directly. 4.6 should say "from a passenger or a customer", and 6.6 should be made expressly subject to it.

MINOR (EN/KA) - the versions carry the same four propositions in the same order, and the terminology is correct throughout (პარტნიორი მძღოლი, დადასტურებული შეკვეთა, ვალდებულია, კომპანია, მგზავრი). One asymmetry sits exactly where the dispute will land: EN 4.5 caps at "the extent STATED in the order" while KA caps at "შეკვეთით განსაზღვრულ ფარგლებს" (the limits DETERMINED by the order). "განსაზღვრული" is a shade wider and could admit limits determined by the Company outside the order text. Given the first defect above, the two signatories would not be arguing the same word; align on მითითებული, or change EN to "determined".

NOTE on the rationale, not the clause text - "a one-way already includes the deadhead return, so in both cases the fee has already paid for the return journey" is overstated. The deadhead line is applyBps(deadheadFull, deadheadRecoveryBps), a recovery SHARE, and the engine's own design note says a city transfer sets recovery near zero. The operative words survive (the return duty only attaches where the order provides a return, and that means directions=2), but this justification should not be repeated to drivers as written.
